## Proof

We prove the statement is **true**: for a linear operator $\rho$ on a Hilbert space,
$$\bigl(\forall\,\sigma\geqslant 0,\; \operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)\geqslant 0\bigr) \iff \rho\geqslant 0.$$

We establish the two implications separately.

### Direction $(\Leftarrow)$: $\rho\geqslant 0 \implies \forall\,\sigma\geqslant 0,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)\geqslant 0$.

Assume $\rho\geqslant 0$ and $\sigma\geqslant 0$. Since $\sigma$ is positive semi-definite, it admits a unique positive semi-definite square root $\sigma^{1/2}\geqslant 0$ with $\sigma = \sigma^{1/2}\sigma^{1/2}$. Using cyclicity of the trace,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma) = \operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\rho\,\sigma^{1/2}\sigma^{1/2}\bigr) = \operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\sigma^{1/2}\rho\,\sigma^{1/2}\bigr).$$
The operator $\sigma^{1/2}\rho\,\sigma^{1/2}$ is positive semi-definite: for any vector $v$,
$$\bigl\langle v\bigm|\sigma^{1/2}\rho\,\sigma^{1/2}\bigm|v\bigr\rangle = \bigl\langle \sigma^{1/2}v\bigm|\rho\bigm|\sigma^{1/2}v\bigr\rangle \geqslant 0,$$
since $\rho\geqslant 0$. The trace of a positive semi-definite operator equals the sum (or supremum of finite partial sums) of its non-negative diagonal entries, hence is non-negative. Therefore
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma) = \operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\sigma^{1/2}\rho\,\sigma^{1/2}\bigr) \geqslant 0. \qquad\checkmark$$

### Direction $(\Rightarrow)$: $\bigl(\forall\,\sigma\geqslant 0,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)\geqslant 0\bigr) \implies \rho\geqslant 0$.

Assume $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)\geqslant 0$ for every positive semi-definite operator $\sigma$. We show $\langle v|\rho|v\rangle \geqslant 0$ for every vector $v$, which is equivalent to $\rho\geqslant 0$.

For any vector $v$, the rank-one operator $\sigma_v := |v\rangle\langle v|$ is positive semi-definite (its only nonzero eigenvalue is $\|v\|^2 \geqslant 0$, with eigenvector $v$). By hypothesis,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\sigma_v) \geqslant 0.$$
We compute this trace. Extend $v/\|v\|$ to an orthonormal basis $\{e_i\}$ (in infinite dimensions, use any orthonormal basis containing the normalized $v$). Then
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,|v\rangle\langle v|) = \sum_i \bigl\langle e_i\bigm|\rho\,|v\rangle\langle v|\bigm|e_i\bigr\rangle = \sum_i \langle e_i|\rho|v\rangle\langle v|e_i\rangle = \bigl\langle v\bigm|\rho\bigm|v\bigr\rangle,$$
where in the last step we used $\sum_i |e_i\rangle\langle e_i| = I$ (resolution of the identity), so $\sum_i \langle e_i|\rho|v\rangle\langle v|e_i\rangle = \langle v|\rho|v\rangle$. (For $v=0$ the result is trivially $0$.)

Hence $\langle v|\rho|v\rangle \geqslant 0$ for all $v$. By definition, this means $\rho\geqslant 0$. $\qquad\checkmark$

### Conclusion

Both directions hold, so the statement is **true**:
$$\forall\,\sigma\geqslant 0,\ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)\geqslant 0 \iff \rho\geqslant 0.$$

The key insight is that rank-one projectors $|v\rangle\langle v|$ are positive semi-definite, so testing against all $\sigma\geqslant 0$ in particular tests against every rank-one projector, which recovers the quadratic form $\langle v|\rho|v\rangle$ and hence fully characterizes positivity of $\rho$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
